intro.lead: I am an AI engineer, and for the past three years I have been building GenAI and machine learning systems that run in production.
intro.rest: I take a system from first prototype to tested, configurable components, and I build the evaluation that shows whether each change helps. I work directly with clients and domain experts on the results. Day to day I build with AI coding agents, and I set up how my team works with them.

howIBuild.title: How I work with AI coding agents
howIBuild.line: Notes on how I use AI coding agents day to day: what works, what does not, and the habits that keep the code mine.
trace: > why did recall drop in the last eval run?
The new threshold drops valid matches. Revert it and rerun?
body: I use AI coding agents every day, at work and in personal projects. Writing code has become cheap, so most of my effort goes into the parts an agent cannot decide for me. That means deciding what the task is and what is in scope, and checking that the result is right. These are the habits that have helped me most so far.
## The agent asks before it works

Most of my agentic tasks start with /clarify-task, a skill I wrote and use at work and in all my personal projects. It takes the agent through four phases: clarify the request, gather context, draft a plan, and wait for my approval. In every phase, the agent has to ask me about anything that is not clear. It is not allowed to guess.

The questions take a few minutes, but they save more time than they cost. I no longer worry whether my prompt covered every detail, because the agent finds the gaps. It also learns what I am trying to achieve, not just what I typed. Since the result already follows my preferences, I spend much less time reviewing and correcting it. This post was planned the same way.
## Public skills, with my own layer on top

I rarely start a setup from nothing. Widely used open-source skills already capture good habits. Two I use are the [Karpathy guidelines](https://github.com/multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills) (think before coding, keep it simple, change only what was asked) and [Ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail) (write the least code the task needs). I adapt them to each project.

On top of them, I add my own layer. It holds my coding and testing guidelines, the project's conventions, structure and style guides, and the style of the text the agent writes for others, such as docs, commit messages and PR descriptions. It also says when the agent should plan, test, commit or stop and ask. The public skills give me a tested baseline, and my layer makes the agent work the way I would.
## One task at a time

While exploring or implementing, an agent often finds things I had not considered. It might be a bug next to the code it is changing, an outdated test, or a rule that no longer makes sense. It is tempting to ask for a fix right away. However, every detour slows the task down and fills the context with unrelated work, and the agent's later work gets worse. The diff also mixes unrelated changes, so it is harder to review, and I lose my own focus.

So I keep each task to its scope. I wrote a skill for this: it notes each finding along the way and turns it into a short brief. Another agent can start from that brief later, without reading the original conversation. Nothing gets lost, and the current task ships first.
## Checking the work

Before I review a change, an agent reviews it. It catches the easy issues, such as bugs, missed edge cases or broken conventions. It does not have the context of the session that wrote the code, so it sees things the first agent missed. It also checks the change against the project's skills and rules. That way my own review can focus on design and logic. I read every diff myself before it merges, and I review better when the diff is small, which is another reason to keep tasks scoped.

Review alone is not enough, though. Every change comes with new or updated tests that must pass, and CI runs them on every change. The tests show that a change works as intended, and they catch side effects that are easy to miss in a diff.
## Learning from corrections

Some tasks need a lot of correcting before they are done. When that happens, I run a skill at the end of the session that goes through every disagreement we had. For each one, it notes what it was about, why it happened, and whether it points to a gap in a skill, a workflow or the project's instructions. Then it makes those changes, so I do not have to make the same correction again.

These fixes go into shared files, not the agent's memory. Memory stays local to me, so it does not help anyone else working on the same code. I also have less control over when memory is updated and what goes into it. A well-defined skill or project rule is clear, and it applies to every contributor and every agent.
## Keeping the context clean

Skills, plugins and workflows pile up quickly. Everything that loads by default takes space in the context window, whether the task needs it or not. Every few weeks, I check what actually loads with the agent's built-in tools (in Claude Code, /context, /doctor and /skill-doctor) and clean up. I turn off unused plugins and skills, merge overlapping ones, shorten long instructions without losing rules, and remove rules that no longer apply. A smaller setup leaves more of the context for the task itself.

caseStudies.title: Mapping free text to a million medical codes
caseStudies.summary: An LLM system that drafts code lists for expert review, with evaluation behind every change.
body: To find patients in health records, you first need to know which codes stand for a disease, a symptom or a treatment. Across the coding systems we work with there are over a million diagnosis, procedure and drug codes, and building these lists by hand was slow and hard to repeat.

I designed and built a GenAI system that drafts these code lists, so experts review a draft instead of starting from nothing. It was first used on a real programme within two months of starting, and since then I have kept improving it for several clients and disease programmes, until it became a tested part of our main platform.

At the start there was no measure of correctness, so every change was a guess. I introduced evaluation against expert-curated golden mappings, with precision and recall per concept, so that prompt and model changes could be compared on evidence. Each matching rule can be switched off, so its contribution can be measured on its own.

Scale was the other problem. A full run compares every concept with every code, which comes to over 100 million concept-code pairs for one programme. The first version ran out of memory after a few thousand codes, so it could only work on small subsets. I rewrote the heavy parts so the system runs on the full set of over a million codes, and checked that in a full-scale simulation before relying on it.

When I moved the system into the platform, I gave it typed configuration, so bad settings fail at start-up, over 1,000 unit tests and an offline mode, so CI runs it end to end without paying for API calls. I also made it serve different clients and coding systems through configuration instead of separate code.

caseStudies.title: ModuGPT and the GenAI tools for log analytics
caseStudies.summary: Master's thesis. An LLM framework and three GenAI tools for searching and explaining logs, shipped to customers.
body: Logmind's platform turns large volumes of logs into insights: the log patterns its models flag as critical. However, an insight still looks like a raw log line, so it is hard to read without knowing the system that wrote it. To look further, users then had to search individual logs with Elasticsearch queries, a language most of them did not know.

I built ModuGPT, a Python framework for LLM tools, and the three tools that shipped on it. I wrote my own instead of using LangChain or LlamaIndex, because each tool needed close control over its calls and fewer layers to debug.

Every tool runs the same steps: check the input, build the prompt, call the model, then check and format the output. Prompts are built from reusable parts such as a persona, rules, a database schema or examples, so a new tool starts from tested pieces. When the model cannot do a task, it answers with a fixed keyword, and the tool returns a clear error instead of a wrong result.

Insight-to-Text explains an insight in plain language and suggests what to check. Users found openings like "This log indicates that..." robotic, so the model always starts that way and the tool removes the phrase, which also confirms that the output has the expected form.
Text-to-ES turns a question into an Elasticsearch query, using the index schema and examples chosen by similarity to the question.

SmartSearch handles questions that mix exact filters with a topic, such as error logs from today related to network problems. A chain of model calls splits the question, sends the exact part through Text-to-ES and the topic through semantic search over log patterns, then combines the two and tells the user how it read the question.

I compared each tool with a control version on 100 examples from five kinds of logs. Where a correct answer exists, I ran the generated query and the expected one and compared the logs they return. Text-to-ES got all 100 queries right, against 13 for a plain prompt. For SmartSearch, the chain raised the score for the exact part from 0.22 to 0.67 compared with a single well-engineered call.

Explanations have no single right answer, so an LLM judge from a different model scored each output in its own prompt, ten times, to limit known judge biases, and the tool won in 95 of 100 cases. The test set had no multi-level aggregations, and those are still harder.

I started with small self-hosted open models, which were too weak for query generation, while larger ones would have needed expensive cloud GPUs. We moved to the OpenAI API, and later to a cheaper model for all tools except Text-to-ES. All of Logmind's GenAI tools were built on ModuGPT and shipped to customers, and the work became my Master's thesis at EPFL. The core framework is public, with the proprietary prompts and tools removed.
